properties.name: A throwaway server on a COPY of the design, launched with --export-to pointed at the real committed record, wrote 8 probe nodes into it — and nothing could have refused, because the copy carries the live design's identity
properties.statement:
HAPPENED 2026-09-12, caught by the loop hint ("the shared record holds 8 node(s) this graph does not: rul:perf-probe-…"), restored from HEAD. An A/B harness measuring the live server's configuration launched a server on a copy of the store with the live flags, including `--export-to ./docs/design/reflow2.json`; the copy's own throwaway writes were auto-exported into the real record.

WHY NO GUARD FIRED, and why one may not be able to: the copy was built by importing the committed export, so it ADOPTED the live design's identity (adopted_identity: reflow2). To the export path the target was legitimately "its" record — same graph id, a lineage it could chain from. A stale-seat refusal compares hashes and the copy was ahead, not behind. The only thing that noticed was the node-count comparison on the NEXT live read.

A LIMIT TO STATE, NOT A DEFECT TO FIX BLINDLY: two stores sharing one identity are by design (that is what an import is for). What might be cheap and honest is for `--export-to` to say at startup, once, which graph directory it will write FROM — so a person reading a harness log sees the mismatch. Recorded as the shape of the trap; no change proposed here.
